topics.title: Understanding dyslexia
topics.intro: What dyslexia is, what it is not, and why it has nothing to do with being smart.

points.text: Dyslexia makes it hard to connect letters to the sounds they make. That makes reading and spelling harder.
Dyslexia has nothing to do with how smart you are.
It is common. Estimates range from about 5 in 100 people to as many as 1 in 5.
Dyslexia is lifelong, but with the right teaching and support, people learn to read and do well in school and work.
Myth: people with dyslexia see letters backwards. Many young children flip letters while learning to write. Most children with dyslexia do not.
Dyslexia is about the sounds of language, not eyesight. Special fonts or glasses are not a treatment. WordWise's font and color settings are there for comfort only.

topics.title: Signs and getting an evaluation
topics.intro: What to look for, and how a professional evaluation works. WordWise cannot diagnose dyslexia.

points.text: Common signs include trouble sounding out words, linking sounds to letters, and spelling, plus slow reading and trouble understanding what was read.
Signs can show up as early as preschool. Dyslexia often runs in families.
An evaluation is usually a set of tests of memory, spelling, visual perception, and reading. Family history and how the child responds to teaching count too.
In U.S. public schools, a full evaluation comes before special education services, and parents must give consent first.
Getting help early leads to better results, but adults can be tested too. It's never too late.

topics.title: School and work accommodations
topics.intro: Extra time, audiobooks, and other changes that let you show what you know.

points.text: Accommodations change how you learn or show what you know. They don't lower expectations or give an unfair advantage.
Examples include extra time on tests, large print, and listening to text in audio form.
In U.S. schools, an IEP gives special teaching and services, and a 504 plan removes barriers in regular classes.
For the PSAT, SAT, and AP exams, accommodations must be requested and approved ahead of time, and it's best to ask through your school.
The ADA requires testing organizations to make exams accessible, and it protects people with disabilities at work.

topics.title: Helpful technology
topics.intro: Tools that read aloud, highlight along, and open up books.

points.text: If you don't know where to start, try text-to-speech, which reads text out loud. WordWise has it built in.
Using assistive technology doesn't keep people from learning to read.
The Library of Congress runs a free audiobook library for people with a reading disability that makes print hard to read.
Bookshare offers accessible ebooks with read-aloud and highlighting for people with qualifying print disabilities, including learning disabilities.
Learning Ally, a nonprofit, offers human-narrated audiobooks for students with dyslexia.

topics.title: For parents and families
topics.intro: How to support a child who finds reading hard, and where to get help.

points.text: Children with dyslexia can get frustrated. Some act out, and some become quiet or withdrawn, at school and at home.
If you're worried, talk to your child's teacher. You can ask the school about an evaluation.
The U.S. has nearly 100 Parent Centers that help families of children with disabilities, from birth to age 26.
With the right teaching, almost all people with dyslexia can learn to read.

topics.title: For adult learners
topics.intro: It's never too late to get answers and support.

points.text: Dyslexia lasts your whole life. If you are diagnosed as an adult, you had it as a child too. It just wasn't noticed.
Adults can get tested, and a diagnosis can help you get the right support at work.
Tools like apps that read text aloud, plus using your strengths, help adults manage dyslexia.
The ADA protects people with disabilities at work, and the EEOC explains how to ask for accommodations.
